title: Four arms, one flip
intro: Same model, same questions, same repo snapshot. Change only how the context reaches the agent and run 48 fresh sessions. One arm cuts structural lookups by a quarter and then doubles the bill on comprehension — and on a small repo every graph arm loses outright.
foot: Every figure is a median of 3 independent fresh claude -p sessions, Sonnet on all arms · raw datasets in expected_output/live-run-multi.json and live-run-priorauth.json

steps.title: One question set, four ways to answer it
narrative: The repo is spring-framework: 9,195 Java files. The question set is four questions, split on purpose into two classes. Structural — "who calls X?" — is answerable from a call graph. Logic — "why does X happen, and by what mechanism?" — needs comprehension.

Four arms differ in exactly one variable each. Baseline is the control: a normal agent, file tools, clean repo. Init adds curated CLAUDE.md files and changes nothing else. Available registers the graph MCP server next to the file tools. Forced takes the file tools away entirely.
Three repetitions per cell, because identical sessions varied by up to 2x. One run is a coin flip; the medians below come from 48 sessions.
steps.youDo: Build the graph and smoke-test the server first: python ../../shared_tools/kg_extract_java.py D:/tmp/spring-framework --out D:/tmp/spring-graph.json --quiet, then run the server standalone and confirm it prints serving over stdio.

after.title: THE RULES THAT MAKE IT A MEASUREMENT

view.text: Baseline runs first, before init ever writes a file into the repo, or the control is contaminated — the runner records repo_claude_md_count per run and warns. Same model, same questions, same snapshot on every arm. And run a forced smoke session before trusting any graph-arm number: it is the only arm with no fallback to hide a dead server behind.

steps.title: Arm 1 — baseline, and it is not the strawman
narrative: The control answered "who calls registerBeanDefinition?" in 3 turns for 116,039 tokens, without opening files wholesale. That is the number every other arm has to beat.

This matters more than it looks. The mechanical benchmark earlier in this capstone predicted a 33.7x advantage for the graph, because it modelled exploration as reading whole files. A real agent's Grep returns matching lines. Any tool that wants to win has to beat line-granular grep, not the whole-file strawman.
steps.youDo: python run_live_bench.py D:/tmp/spring-framework --arms baseline --reps 3 — first, on a clean repo, before anything else touches it.

terminal.text: S1 baseline  rep0 5t 167,742  rep1 3t 116,039  rep2 3t 112,982   median 3t 116,039

steps.title: Arm 2 — init: a map, not an index
narrative: Generate a CLAUDE.md for each of the 22 spring-* modules, change nothing else, and re-run. The average is a wash: 600K, +2%, plus a one-time generation cost of about $3.40.

The average hides the story. On S1 the curated map sent the agent straight to the right module — 81,352 tokens in 2 turns, a 30% win. On S2 the same auto-loaded context never paid for itself: +58%. It helps most on the logic side, where orientation is the bottleneck, at 321K, −7%.
The read: a CLAUDE.md is orientation and conventions, not a lookup index. It pays when the session's first problem is "where do I even start?" and taxes you when it isn't.
steps.youDo: python init_claude_mds.py D:/tmp/spring-framework --prefix spring-, run the arm, then --remove to restore the clean repo. Note the gotcha: /init does not fire in claude -p mode, so the script issues an explicit "analyze this module and Write CLAUDE.md" instruction instead.

steps.title: Arm 3 — available: paying for both paths
narrative: This is the integration almost everyone actually ships: register the graph MCP server alongside the normal tools and tell the model to prefer it. The model chooses.
It was the worst arm in the campaign on structural questions: 570K, +137%. On S2 it burned 10 turns and 415,455 tokens — worse than having no graph at all.

The mechanism is not stupidity. The model queried the graph, got back a bare-name answer with over a thousand candidates, correctly did not trust it, and re-verified against files. It paid for both retrieval paths. That distrust is rational given a teaching-grade graph's AMBIGUOUS fan-out; a type-resolved production graph earns trust by answering compactly.

steps.title: Arm 4 — forced: one turn, 41,824 tokens
narrative: Take the file tools away. The graph is the only search surface, and the prompt tells the model to note honestly where AMBIGUOUS provenance leaves it uncertain.

S1 came back in one turn for 41,824 tokens — 64% under baseline. Across both structural questions the arm landed at 178K, −26%: the only arm in the campaign that beat the control on structural lookups.

The finding is not "graphs are cheaper". It is that forcing is what unlocks the win. Remove the option to double-check and the graph's one-call answers finally beat grep — which is precisely why the available arm, same graph and same model, lost by 137%.
steps.youDo: python run_live_bench.py D:/tmp/spring-framework --arms forced --reps 3 --mcp-config mcp.json. Run this arm before you trust any other graph-arm number — with no file tools to fall back on, a broken server says so out loud.

steps.title: The flip: same arm, logic questions, +120%
narrative: Now ask the winner a question a call graph was never built to answer. "Why can registerBeanDefinition throw BeanDefinitionOverrideException?" The forced agent got it right — it walked callee edges and reconstructed the override-guard chain — in 12 turns for 523,791 tokens, against baseline's 6 turns and 231,012, which included simply reading the file.
Across both logic questions: 758K, +120%. The graph can substitute for reading code, expensively. It cannot beat reading code at comprehension.

One confound reported rather than buried: Spring is in the model's training data, so edge-walking partly confirmed logic it already knew. On a private codebase that same graph-shaped confidence over unread code is a hallucination risk, not a capability.
steps.youDo: Add --forced-logic to include the "why" questions in the forced arm — it is the expensive run, and it is the one that produces this finding.

answers correct in both — cost, not accuracy, is what moved

before.title: NO ARM WINS EVERYWHERE — THAT IS THE FINDING

after.title: THE SYNTHESIS — M10's ROUTER, DERIVED FROM DATA

view.text: Route structural questions to the forced graph and everything else to files: 178K + 345K ≈ 523K for this question set, against 585K all-baseline. Each layer serves only the question class it is good at. Two honesty notes to carry with the table: the forced arm's dollar-cost field did not reconcile with its usage fields, so tokens and turns are the trustworthy columns there; and S2 under forcing had wild spread (45K–698K) because bare-name resolution merges overloads into thousand-caller answers.

steps.title: The counterpoint: 36 files, and every graph arm loses
narrative: Same four scenarios, same methodology, another 48 sessions — on priorauth-api-boot3, a 36-file Spring Boot service. The verdict flips completely.

One 55-line root CLAUDE.md is the best arm overall at 565K, −10%, and −38% on the orientation-heavy logic question, where the map pointed straight at CriteriaScoringService. The graph loses in every configuration — including forced, at +84%. At 36 files grep answers a caller question in two turns, the graph is tiny and half AMBIGUOUS, and forced edge-walking burned 17 to 18 turns on the "why" questions.

This is the roughly 500-file payoff floor measured live instead of asserted, and it is the sharpest form of the course's closing lesson: which context lever wins is a property of the repo and the question mix, not of the tool. Big haystack plus structural questions, force the graph. Small repo one person can hold in their head, write one good CLAUDE.md. The only way to know which world you are in is the measurement you just learned to run.
steps.youDo: Run the same campaign on your own repo. Report your grid with the arm definitions attached — a token multiple without an integration mode and a question mix beside it is not a result.
